### Upadaya = the absolutive of upadana (relativity)
"Upadaya is the absolutive form of upadana, it has the implication of
something relative... This holding on creates a certain relationship,
which may be technically termed a relativity. The two stand relative to
each other."
"The prefix upa in upadana conveys the sense of proximity or nearness...
So the totality of existence, from the point of view of Dhamma, is
dependent on a holding on, or a grasping on."

### The mirror simile (Punna Mantaniputta, Khandha-samyutta)
"It is with dependence, friend Ananda, that the notion 'am' occurs, not
without dependence. With dependence on form... on feeling... on
perception... on preparations... on consciousness does the notion 'am'
occur."
"Just as a woman or a man, youthful and fond of adornment, in looking
at her or his facial image in a mirror or in a bowl filled with pure,
clear, clean water, would be seeing it with dependence and not without
dependence."
Analayo parallel: SĀ 261.
"It is when one looks into a mirror that one suddenly becomes self-
conscious... Even if one already has no such notion, the moment one looks
into a mirror one is suddenly reminded of it, as if to exclaim: 'Ah,
here I am!'"

### The twenty modes of personality view
"As regards form, it is fourfold: He regards form as self, or self as
possessing form, or form as in self, or self as in form. It is the same
with the other four groups. In this way, the personality view is
altogether twenty-fold."
"All this comes about due to the ignorance that name-and-form is only a
reflection, like that facial image."

### The whirlpool mapped to the twelve links
"The ignorance in presuming that it is possible to go against the main
stream of the three signata — impermanence, suffering and not-self — is
the place of its origin. That heap of preparations impelled by ignorance,
which takes the current forward, may be regarded as sankharas. And where
the current in its progress clashes with the main stream to become a
whirlpool, that pushing forward against the main stream is vinnana or
consciousness. The outcome of the clash is nama-rupa, or name-and-form,
with its formal name and nominal form."

### The abyss = painful bodily feelings
"Monks, abyss is a synonym for painful bodily feelings." (Bodhi: "bottom-
less abyss.") The uninstructed worldling "sorrows, grieves, and laments;
he weeps and beats his breast and becomes distraught. This is called an
uninstructed worldling who has not risen up in the bottomless abyss, one
who has not gained a foothold." Chinese parallel: CBETA T02 no. 99.

### Salatana = the abyss; craving = the thirst to quell it
"The thirst of craving arises in beings in various forms of existence
because of painful feeling. The uninstructed worldling, on being touched
by painful feeling, delights in sense pleasures, because he knows no way
out of painful feeling other than the sense pleasures. The abyss is the
endless barrage of painful feelings. The force of attraction that arises
from the abyss is like the thirst to quell those painful feelings."

### The Dhamma-eye = seeing the solution in the problem
"What is called the 'Dhamma-eye', is the ability to see the Nibbanic
solution in the very vortex of the samsaric problem. That way of analysis
which puts samsara and Nibbana far apart, into two watertight
compartments, as it were, gives rise to interminable problems.

### The fumigating verb (vidhūpeti / sandhūpeti)
"The Buddha also had to stage a similar fire ordeal in the Dhammayāga,
or the 'Dhamma-sacrifice', he administered to exorcize the malignant
personality view, sakkāyadiṭṭhi, ingrained in the minds of worldlings."
"The word vidhūpeti, derived from the word dhūpa, 'incense', is
suggestive of 'fumigating' or 'smoking out'."
Bodhivagga (Udāna): "When dhammas manifest themselves, to the
resolutely meditating Brahmin, he stands fumigating the hordes of Māra,
like the sun irradiating the firmament."
"While some fragrant kinds of incense are used for propitiating
benevolent spirits, certain caustic types are utilized for exorcising
evil spirits... the phrase could be rendered as 'he exorcises and does
not propitiate'." (Khajjanīyasutta)

### Flotsam after the vortex ceases
"The ordinary worldling's mode of recognition of the Tathāgata is
comparable to the recognition of a vortex that has already ceased with
the help of the flotsam and jetsam lightly floating around it. Even
after the vortex has ceased, flotsam and jetsam could still go on
rotating, giving the wrong impression that the vortex is still there."
"If one understands that the vortex has actually ceased deep down at
its centre, and that what remains there, now, is the great ocean...
one can get rid of the unfounded fear arising from the statement that
there is no Tathāgata in truth and fact."
"The cessation of the puny centre of the whirlpool is equivalent to
inheriting an expansive great ocean. To give up the limitations of a
vortex, is to inherit the limitless ocean."

### The six sense-bases as six measuring rods
"There are six modes of measuring in accordance with the conceit 'am',
asmimāna. What is known as saḷāyatana, or the six sense-bases,

### Yoniso manasikāra = attention by way of source
"Strictly speaking, yoniso manasikāra, or 'radical reflection', is
attention by way of source or matrix."
"The bodhisatta Vipassī went on reflecting from the very end of the
formula of paṭicca samuppāda, of dependent arising, in reverse order
and gradually arrived at the true source."
"Kimhi nu kho sati jarāmaraṇaṃ hoti, kiṃ paccayā jarāmaraṇaṃ?
Jātiyā kho sati jarāmaraṇaṃ hoti, jātipaccayā jarāmaraṇaṃ — 'What
being there, does decay and death come to be? Conditioned by what, is
decay-and-death? Birth being there does decay-and-death come to be,
conditioned by birth.'"
"In this way, he directed his radical reflection gradually upwards...
and at last came to the saṃsāric vortex between consciousness and
name-and-form."
"This is an illustration of the deepest sense of yoniso manasikāra as
an attitude essential for seeing the law of dependent arising within
one's own experience." (Mahāpadānasutta)

### The Sūciloma recap: from within
"This ito, 'hence', means from within one's self. This is clear from
the term attasambhūta, 'self-begotten'."
"They are revealed only to radical reflection, to attention by way of
source or matrix. That is why the Buddha emphasizes the need for
discerning the true source."
"And they that know wherefrom it springs, they dispel it... they
cross this flood so hard to cross, never crossed before, to become no
more."
Analayo parallel: Bodhi (2017: 201).

### The true source is ignorance, not craving
"The commentary takes the term yatonidānaṃ in this verse as a
reference to the second noble truth of craving... But it is actually an
allusion to ignorance. The true source is non-understanding. That is
why the Buddha... went beyond craving and placed ignorance at the head
of the series of twelve links.

### The three-lives vs one-mind-moment framework
Header: Patisambhidamagga / Vibhanga / Jnanaprasthana / Mahavibhasa.
The sermon addresses whether dependent origination reads across three
lives or within one mind-moment. Both frames are valid.

### The itthabhava/annathabhava circuit
"This-ness and otherwise-ness imply a circuit. It is a circuit between
a 'here' and a 'there'. It is a turning round, an alternation or a
circuitous journey. It is like a rotation on the spot. It is an
ambivalence between a here and a there."

### Consciousness travel = change of point of view
"The passage of consciousness from here to a mother's womb is not a
movement from one place to another, as in the case of the body. In
reality, it is only a difference of point of view, and not a transmigration
of a soul."
"When consciousness leaves this body and comes to stay in a mother's
womb, when it is fully established there, 'that' place becomes a 'this'
place. From the point of view of that consciousness, the 'there' becomes
a 'here'. Consequently, from the new point of view, what was earlier a
'here', becomes a 'there'."
"That way, what actually is involved here, is a change of point of view.
So it does not mean completely leaving one place and going to another,
as is usually meant by the journey of an individual. The process, then,
is a sort of going round and round."

### The thirty-six pathways of beings (Saḷāyatanavibhaṅga)
"Chattiṃsa sattapadā, literally 'thirty-six steps of beings'":
six happiness based on household life; six happiness based on
renunciation; six unhappiness household; six unhappiness renunciation;
six equanimity household; six equanimity renunciation — each "six" =
form, sound, smell, taste, tangible, idea.
Analayo parallel: Ñāṇamoli (1995: 1067–1071); MĀ 163.

### The four definitions (paradigm: form)
Household happiness: "When one regards as an acquisition an
acquisition of forms... desirable, charming, agreeable, delightful,
connected with worldly gains, or when one recalls what was formerly
acquired that has passed, ceased and changed, happiness arises."
Renunciation happiness: "When by knowing the impermanence, change,
fading away and cessation of forms one sees as it actually is with
right wisdom... happiness arises. Such happiness... is called
happiness based on renunciation."
Household unhappiness: non-acquisition and lost recollection.
Renunciation unhappiness: "One arouses a longing for the supreme
deliverances thus: 'When shall I enter upon and abide in that sphere
that the Noble Ones now enter upon and abide in?' In one who arouses
such a longing... unhappiness arises conditioned by that longing."
Household equanimity: "Equanimity arises in a foolish infatuated
worldling... such equanimity as this does not transcend form."
Renunciation equanimity: "Equanimity arises... Such equanimity as this
transcends form."

### The five declarations as a staged tetralemma
1. "Whatever is seen, heard, sensed and cognized... that I know" —
   yet "the Tathāgata has not taken his stand upon it."
2. "If I were to say 'all that I do not know', it would be a falsehood
   in me."
3. "If I were to say 'I both know it and do not know it', that too
   would be a falsehood in me."
4. "If I were to say 'I neither know it, nor am ignorant of it', it
   would be a fault in me."
"The Tathāgata has no stance, not because he is ignorant, but due to
the very fact that he knows full well and has understood the nature of
the sum total of sensory data."
"So it seems, in this context too, we have the negation of the first
alternative, as is usual in the case of a tetralemma, only that the
negation is expressed here in a very peculiar way."

### The reading dispute (na jānāmī vs jānāmī)
"The commentary has followed the reading tam ahaṃ 'jānāmī'ti
vadeyyaṃ... But as we have pointed out earlier, this reading is not
meaningful. That is probably why the Chaṭṭhasaṅgīti-piṭaka edition has
followed the variant reading tam ahaṃ 'na jānāmī'ti vadeyyaṃ."

### The eel-wriggler rejected (Sañjaya Belaṭṭhiputta)
"This attitude of wriggling out had already assumed the status of a
philosophy in itself in Sañjaya Belaṭṭhiputta, a contemporary of the
Buddha... he would respond with such a series of negations like 'I do
not say it is, I do not say it is thus, I do not say it is otherwise,
nor do I say it is neither'... The attempt here is to evade the issue
by a sort of 'eel-wriggling'. That school of philosophy, which resorted
to such an evasive legerdemain, came to be known as
amarā-vikkhepa-vāda. The Buddha refuses to subscribe to such tactical
sophistry."
